entries.label: Tell us how you heard about Zipline and this job!
Are you available for a full-time onsite internship this spring (January 2027 - April 2027)?
Why are you interested in becoming an Enterprise Systems Software Engineering Intern?
entries.value: The work I keep coming back to is software that sits inside a real operational workflow, where a wrong output has a physical consequence. At Intelehealth I built a resource-availability scoring pipeline in Python across 32 villages, combining facility-tier classification, geospatial distance, Google Maps data, weather, and healthcare-resource availability to support care decisions in rural settings. What stuck with me was how much of the difficulty was logistical rather than modeling: whether a clinic was reachable mattered more than any clever feature. Zipline is solving that problem at a much larger scale, with deliveries somewhere in the world every 30 seconds across four continents, and enterprise systems are the layer that makes that scale legible to the people running it. I also care about determinism in operational software. In a job-application agent I built, every application moves through an explicit state machine and every mutating capability sits behind fail-closed flags, because state that can silently diverge is how automation causes real damage. That instinct seems directly relevant to internal systems that operations, fulfillment, and finance actually depend on.

entries.label: Tell us about a project where something didn’t work as expected. What was the problem and how did you figure out what to do next?
entries.value: Over the past year I studied how scientific research gets funded and evaluated, and I started with a strong hypothesis: the main constraint on science was grant-writing time and administrative burden. I read papers and institutional history, then interviewed researchers, research administrators, economists, and people building alternative research organizations. The interviews contradicted me. Several people had consciously traded compensation and overhead for autonomy over what they worked on, so my compensation story was too simple. I now think the more important effect is selection: researchers learn which ideas are legible enough to survive review, and never attempt the ones that are hard to justify in advance. I also explored building automated reproducibility checks for published papers. Technically it was appealing, but the idea fell apart when I asked who would actually pay for a system whose main output is problems in work that is already published. Instead of forcing that product, I moved toward the question I now think is real: if AI makes scientific generation cheap, evaluation and judgment become the scarce resource, and that is a technical problem worth building for.
entries.reason: Essay generated from the operator's about-me context

entries.label: Describe a recent project where you used AI tools while building software. What did the AI help with, and what parts still required your judgement?
entries.value: I built tSearch, a talent-discovery system that starts from named seed candidates, expands through public collaboration and publishing graphs like GitHub and Substack, and assesses evidence of actual building rather than school or employer prestige. LLMs do the assessment layer: rubric-driven judges evaluate separate dimensions in parallel and then synthesize a final assessment that has to cite the evidence it used. That part is genuinely well suited to a model, since it is reading messy public text and applying a rubric. The parts I refused to hand over were the ones where a model failure would quietly corrupt the output. Identity resolution and graph expansion stay separate from judging, so an LLM cannot silently paper over a case where I matched the wrong person or re-run discovery to justify a score. The heuristic discovery score is not collapsed into the LLM assessment score. I also made missing evidence resolve to "insufficient evidence" instead of a low score, because a model asked to grade a dimension will produce a number whether or not the underlying evidence exists. Choosing where the model is allowed to conclude anything was the design work.

entries.label: Tell us about the most technically challenging project you’ve built. What problem were you solving, what decisions did you make, and what would you do differently today?
entries.value: The hardest system I have worked on is the machine-learning core of an anomaly-detection and alert-prioritization product at Summer Atlantic Capital. I own major parts of the data and ML infrastructure: the repository and CI scaffold, the event-ingestion pipeline, a versioned FastAPI microservice, and the public detection API. The modeling side does temporal sequence modeling over event streams with RNN and Transformer-style approaches, anomaly scoring, and a learning-to-rank layer on top. The decision I care most about was treating alert volume as part of the problem rather than a downstream concern. An anomaly detector that fires constantly hands the analyst a second problem instead of solving the first, so ranking and an LLM explanation layer built on retrieval-augmented generation were part of the design rather than additions. What I would do differently is sequence it the other way. I built detection quality first and then worked on prioritization and explanation. If I started again, I would define what a useful analyst-facing output looks like, and the failure modes I need to document, before tuning the model, because that definition changes what I optimize.
